The answer is no, guitars don't sound better as they age.

But, that's just a general rule. Some guitars sound better with age and some manufacturers pay a great deal of attention to their work, such as Martin. Martins are built with wood with known qualities and they know how much moisture the wood will keep and how there's an optimal range, and those guitars "mature" after about 20 years - which means they sound better with age.

But...

Many guitars have a distinctive voice. Many artists want to use that distinctive voice. I can sometimes guess the approximate age of a GLP just from hearing it play without any distractions.

There's also selection bias...

When people say, "A 1953 Martin D-28 sounds fantastic!" They're not paying attention to the fact that there's probably fewer than 500 remaining, out of a 2500 that were manufactured. The ones that remain were kept in ideal conditions - or may actually not even sound that good.

There is, however, some guitars that do sound better with age. Wood's complicated and guitars are placed into a variety of shitty environments.
Thanks very much for that in depth response!

Yeah, it is a bit complicated.

A good example might be, "I played a Martin at the music store. I don't see why it's worth that much money." I see that with some regularity.

You buy a Martin because it will still sound excellent in 20 years and, sometimes, will even sound better - because the wood will have settled down and reached an optimal point to get the resonance and richness of tone that people are familiar with. When they're new, they sound pretty much like a guitar that's 3/4 of the retail price.

It's also subjective as hell, and genre specific. What sounds better to me may not actually sound better to you. What gives a more full tone to classical guitar style music might not be as appreciated by fans or an artist preferring a punchier sound for something like rock or bluegrass.
